div.head: Section 17
div.p: How you, men of Athens, have been affected by my accusers, I do not know. But I myself was almost carried away by them, so persuasively did they speak. And yet, hardly a single word they said was true. But among their many falsehoods, one amazed me most of all: they said you should be careful not to be deceived by me, because I am a formidable speaker. That they were not ashamed to be immediately refuted by the facts, the moment I show myself not to be a formidable speaker in the slightest—that seemed to me their most shameless act. Unless, of course, they call a formidable speaker the one who speaks the truth. If that is what they mean, I would agree that I am an orator, though not of their sort. Well, as I say, they have spoken hardly a word of truth; but from me, you shall hear the whole truth. Not, by Zeus, men of Athens, speeches beautifully crafted with phrases and words, arranged like theirs. No, you will hear things spoken simply, with whatever words come to mind, for I believe that what I say is just. Let none of you expect anything else. For it would certainly not be fitting, men of Athens, at my age, to come before you like a youth, weaving fine speeches. But I do make this one great request and plea to you, men of Athens: if you hear me making my defense using the same words I am accustomed to use in the marketplace by the bankers' tables, where many of you have heard me, and elsewhere, do not be surprised and do not make a disturbance on that account. For the situation is this: this is the first time I have ever come before a law court, though I am seventy years old. Therefore, I am simply a stranger to the manner of speaking here. Just as if I were truly a foreigner, you would surely excuse me if I spoke in the dialect and manner in which I had been raised, so I now ask this just request of you, as it seems to me: disregard the manner of my speech—perhaps it may be worse, perhaps better—and consider this one thing alone, and apply your mind to this: whether the things I say are just or not. For this is the virtue of a judge, while the virtue of an orator is to speak the truth.

div.head: Section 18
div.p: First, then, it is just for me to defend myself against the first false accusations made against me, and my first accusers; and after that, against the later ones. For many have accused me before you for many years now, and not a word they said was true. I fear these men more than Anytus and his companions, though they too are formidable. But the earlier ones are more formidable, men of Athens. They took hold of the majority of you from childhood and persuaded you of their accusations against me, none of which are true: that there is a certain Socrates, a wise man, a thinker on things aloft, who has investigated all things under the earth, and who makes the weaker argument the stronger. These men, men of Athens, who have spread this rumor, are my formidable accusers. For those who hear them believe that men who investigate such things do not even believe in the gods. Moreover, these accusers are many, and they have been accusing me for a long time. Furthermore, they spoke to you at an age when you were most likely to believe them, when some of you were children and youths, simply winning a case by default, as there was no one to make a defense. And the most unreasonable thing of all is that it is not even possible to know and name them, except perhaps for a certain comic poet. All those who, through envy and slander, persuaded you—and those who, having been persuaded themselves, persuaded others—all these are completely out of reach. For it is not possible to call any of them here to the stand or to cross-examine them; I must literally fight with shadows in making my defense and cross-examine when no one answers. Therefore, you must also assume, as I say, that my accusers are of two kinds: those who have accused me recently, and those of old whom I am talking about now. And you must agree that I should defend myself against the earlier ones first, for you heard them accusing me much earlier, and much more often, than the later ones. Very well. A defense must be made, men of Athens, and I must attempt, in this short time, to remove from you the prejudice that you have held for a long time. I wish this might happen, if it is better for both you and me, and that I might achieve something by my defense. But I think it is difficult, and I am not at all unaware of its nature. Nevertheless, let the outcome proceed as the god pleases; I must obey the law and make my defense.

div.head: Section 19
div.p: Let us examine from the beginning what the accusation is from which the slander against me has arisen, the very slander Meletus trusted when he wrote this indictment against me. What did the slanderers say to slander me? We must read their sworn statement, as if they were official accusers: "Socrates acts unjustly and is a meddler, investigating the things beneath the earth and the heavenly bodies, making the weaker argument the stronger, and teaching these same things to others." It is something like this. You yourselves saw these things in the comedy of Aristophanes: a certain Socrates swinging around up there, claiming he was walking on air and spouting a great deal of other nonsense about matters of which I have no knowledge, great or small. And I do not say this to disparage such knowledge, if anyone is wise in such things—may I never be prosecuted by Meletus on charges of such magnitude!—but the fact is, men of Athens, I have no share in these matters. I offer the majority of you as witnesses to this, and I ask you to inform and tell each other, as many of you as have ever heard me conversing—and there are many of you. Tell each other, then, if any of you has ever heard me conversing about such matters, either briefly or at length. And from this you will know that the other things the multitude says about me are of the same nature. But in fact, none of this is true. And if you have heard from anyone that I undertake to educate people and charge money for it, that is not true either. Though it seems to me to be a fine thing if a man is actually able to educate people, like Gorgias of Leontini, Prodicus of Ceos, and Hippias of Elis. Each of these men, gentlemen, is able to go into any city and persuade the young men—who could associate with any of their own citizens for free—to leave the company of their fellow citizens, associate with them instead, pay them money, and be grateful besides.

div.head: Section 20
div.p: Indeed, there is another wise man here from Paros, who I learned was in town. For I happened to meet a man who has spent more money on sophists than all the others combined—Callias, the son of Hipponicus. I asked him (for he has two sons): "Callias," I said, "if your two sons were colts or calves, we could find and hire an overseer for them who would make them fine and good in their proper virtue, and he would be a horse trainer or a farmer. But since they are human beings, whom do you intend to hire as an overseer for them? Who is knowledgeable in such virtue, the virtue of a human being and a citizen? I assume you have considered this since you have sons. Is there anyone," I asked, "or not?" "Certainly," he said. "Who is he," I asked, "and where is he from, and for how much does he teach?" "Evenus, Socrates," he said. "From Paros, for five minae." And I considered Evenus blessed, if he truly possesses this art and teaches it so suitably. As for me, I would pride myself and put on airs if I knew these things. But the truth is, I do not know them, men of Athens. Perhaps one of you might interrupt and say, "But Socrates, what is your occupation? Where did these slanders against you come from? For surely all this rumor and talk would not have arisen if you were doing nothing out of the ordinary, but only if you were doing something different from most people. Tell us what it is, so that we do not judge you rashly." The man who says this seems to me to be speaking justly, and I will try to show you what has caused my reputation and the slander against me. Listen, then. And perhaps some of you will think I am joking, but rest assured, I will tell you the whole truth. I have gained this reputation, men of Athens, from nothing else but a certain kind of wisdom. What kind of wisdom is this? Perhaps it is merely human wisdom. For in this, I really might be wise. The men I just mentioned might be wise in some wisdom greater than human, or I don't know what to call it. I certainly do not know it, and whoever says I do is lying and speaking to slander me. And do not make a disturbance, men of Athens, even if I seem to be boasting to you. For the word I shall speak is not my own; I shall refer you to a speaker worthy of your trust. Concerning my wisdom, whether it is wisdom at all and of what kind, I shall offer you the god at Delphi as a witness.

div.head: Section 21
div.p: You surely knew Chaerephon. He was a friend of mine from youth, and a friend to your democratic multitude; he went into exile with you recently and returned with you. You know what kind of man Chaerephon was, how impetuous he was in whatever he undertook. Well, he once went to Delphi and dared to ask the oracle this question—now, as I say, please do not make a disturbance, gentlemen. He asked if there was anyone wiser than I. The Pythia replied that there was no one wiser. His brother here will testify to these things before you, since Chaerephon himself is dead. Now consider why I am telling you this. I am going to explain to you where the slander against me came from. When I heard this, I reasoned with myself as follows: "What does the god mean? What is his riddle? For I know very well that I am not wise, either greatly or slightly. What then does he mean by saying I am the wisest? Surely he is not lying; for it is not lawful for him to do so." For a long time I was at a loss as to what he meant. Then, with great reluctance, I turned to investigating the matter in this way: I went to one of the men who are reputed to be wise, thinking that there, if anywhere, I could refute the oracle and say to it, "This man is wiser than I, but you said I was." So I examined this man—I need not mention his name by name, but he was one of our politicians—and when I examined him and conversed with him, men of Athens, this was my experience: it seemed to me that this man seemed wise to many other people, and especially to himself, but he was not. Then I tried to show him that he thought himself wise, but was not. As a result, I became hateful to him and to many of those present. As I went away, I reasoned with myself: "I am wiser than this man. It is likely that neither of us knows anything noble and good, but he thinks he knows something when he does not, while I, since I do not know, do not think I know. I seem, then, to be slightly wiser than him in just this one small thing: that what I do not know, I do not think I know." After this, I went to another man, one of those reputed to be wiser than the first, and the exact same thing seemed to me to be true. And there I became hateful to him and to many others.

div.head: Section 22
div.p: After that I went to others in succession, realizing with sorrow and fear that I was becoming hated. Yet I thought it necessary to place the greatest importance on the word of the god. I had to go to all those reputed to know something, investigating what the oracle meant. And by the dog, men of Athens—for I must tell you the truth—this was roughly my experience: as I investigated according to the god's command, those with the highest reputations seemed to me to be the most deficient, while others who were considered inferior seemed to be superior men when it came to intelligence. I must display my wandering to you, like a man performing labors, only to finally prove the oracle irrefutable. After the politicians, I went to the poets—writers of tragedies, dithyrambs, and the others—expecting that there I would catch myself red-handed being more ignorant than they. Picking up the poems they seemed to have worked on the most, I asked them what they meant, so that I might learn something from them at the same time. I am ashamed to tell you the truth, gentlemen, but it must be told. Almost everyone present could have spoken better about the poems than the men who had composed them. So I soon realized about the poets too, that it was not by wisdom that they made what they made, but by some natural genius and inspiration, like seers and prophets; for they too say many fine things, but know nothing of what they say. The poets seemed to me to be in a similar state. And at the same time, I perceived that because of their poetry, they thought they were the wisest of men in other things as well, which they were not. So I left them, thinking that I was superior to them by the same margin as I was to the politicians. Finally, I went to the craftsmen. I was conscious that I knew practically nothing myself, but I knew that I would find them possessing knowledge of many fine things. And in this I was not deceived: they did know things I did not know, and in that way they were wiser than I. But, men of Athens, the good craftsmen seemed to me to suffer from the same flaw as the poets: because they performed their art well, each of them claimed to be the wisest in other, the most important matters—and this discord of theirs overshadowed that other wisdom. So I asked myself, on behalf of the oracle, whether I would prefer to be exactly as I am—neither wise in their wisdom nor ignorant in their ignorance—or to have both of what they have. And I answered myself and the oracle that it was to my advantage to be exactly as I am.

div.head: Section 23
div.p: From this investigation, men of Athens, many enmities have arisen against me, and of the most harsh and burdensome kind, resulting in many slanders and the title of being "wise." For those present on each occasion suppose that I myself am wise in whatever subject I refute someone else. But in truth, gentlemen, the god is likely wise, and in this oracle he means that human wisdom is worth little or nothing. He appears to be speaking of Socrates, using my name as an example, as if he were to say: "This man among you, O mortals, is the wisest, who, like Socrates, has recognized that he is truly worthless concerning wisdom." This is why even now I go about investigating and examining anyone, citizen or foreigner, whom I think is wise, according to the god's command. And when he seems to me not to be wise, I assist the god by showing him that he is not wise. Because of this occupation, I have had no time for any public affairs worth mentioning, nor any private ones, but I live in extreme poverty because of my service to the god. In addition to this, the young men who have the most leisure, the sons of the wealthiest men, follow me around of their own accord. They enjoy hearing men being cross-examined, and they often imitate me and attempt to examine others. And I imagine they find a great abundance of men who think they know something but know little or nothing. Consequently, those who are examined by them become angry with me, not with themselves, and say that "Socrates is a most pestilential fellow who corrupts the youth." When someone asks them what he does and what he teaches to corrupt them, they have nothing to say, because they do not know. But so as not to seem at a loss, they repeat the standard charges brought against all philosophers: "the things aloft and under the earth," "not believing in gods," and "making the weaker argument the stronger." For I think they would not be willing to speak the truth: that they have been exposed as pretending to know when they know nothing. Because they are ambitious, forceful, and numerous, and because they speak concertedly and persuasively about me, they have filled your ears with harsh and persistent slander for a long time. From these ranks Meletus, Anytus, and Lycon attacked me. Meletus is aggrieved on behalf of the poets, Anytus on behalf of the craftsmen and politicians, and Lycon on behalf of the orators. So, as I began by saying, I would be amazed if I were able to remove from you, in this short time, a prejudice that has grown so large.

div.head: Section 24
div.p: This is the truth, men of Athens, and I am speaking to you hiding nothing, neither great nor small, and holding nothing back. Though I know very well that I make myself hated by doing this. But that is the proof that I am speaking the truth, and that this is the slander against me, and these are its causes. Whether you investigate these matters now or later, you will find it to be so. Let this be a sufficient defense before you against the charges made by my first accusers. Next I will try to defend myself against Meletus, that "good and patriotic man," as he calls himself, and the later accusers. Let us again take up their sworn statement, as if they were a different set of accusers. It runs something like this: it says Socrates acts unjustly by corrupting the youth and by not believing in the gods the city believes in, but in other new spiritual things. Such is the charge. Let us examine each point of this accusation. He says I act unjustly by corrupting the youth. But I say, men of Athens, that Meletus acts unjustly because he jests in serious matters, eagerly bringing men to trial, pretending to be serious and concerned about matters he has never cared about at all. I will try to show you that this is the case. Come here, Meletus, and tell me: do you not consider it of the utmost importance that the young men be as good as possible?
MELETUS. I do.

SOCRATES. Come then, tell these men, who makes them better? For clearly you know, since you care about it. Having discovered the one who corrupts them—me, as you say—you are bringing me before these judges and accusing me. Come, name the one who makes them better, and tell them who he is. Do you see, Meletus, that you are silent and have nothing to say? Does this not seem shameful to you, and a sufficient proof of exactly what I say, that you have never cared about this? Tell me, my good man, who makes them better?
MELETUS. The laws.
SOCRATES. That is not what I am asking, my excellent friend. I am asking what man, who first knows this very thing, the laws.
MELETUS. These judges here, Socrates.
SOCRATES. What do you mean, Meletus? Are these men able to educate the youth and make them better?
MELETUS. Most certainly.
SOCRATES. All of them? Or some of them and not others?
MELETUS. All of them.

div.head: Section 25
div.p: SOCRATES. Well said, by Hera, and a great abundance of benefactors! What about the audience listening here? Do they make them better or not?
MELETUS. They do too.
SOCRATES. And the members of the Council?
MELETUS. The Councillors as well.
SOCRATES. But Meletus, what about the men in the Assembly? Do the Assemblymen corrupt the youth, or do they all make them better too?
MELETUS. They make them better too.
SOCRATES. So it seems that all the Athenians make them beautiful and good, except for me. I alone corrupt them. Is this what you say?
MELETUS. That is exactly what I say, most forcefully.

SOCRATES. You have condemned me to a great misfortune! But answer me: does it seem to be the same way with horses? Do all men make them better, while a single individual corrupts them? Or is it the exact opposite: one individual, or a very few—the horse trainers—are able to make them better, while the majority, if they deal with horses and use them, corrupt them? Is this not so, Meletus, both for horses and for all other animals? It certainly is, whether you and Anytus agree or deny it. For it would be a great blessing for the youth if only one man corrupts them, and all the rest benefit them. But, Meletus, you have sufficiently shown that you have never given any thought to the youth. You have clearly displayed your own lack of care, showing that you care nothing for the matters you indicted me for. Now tell us further, Meletus, before Zeus, whether it is better to live among good citizens or bad ones? Answer, my friend, for I am not asking anything difficult. Do not bad citizens do evil to those closest to them, while good ones do good?
MELETUS. Certainly.
SOCRATES. Is there anyone who wishes to be harmed by those he associates with rather than benefited? Answer, my good man, for the law commands you to answer. Is there anyone who wishes to be harmed?
MELETUS. Of course not.
SOCRATES. Come then, do you bring me to trial here claiming that I corrupt the youth and make them worse intentionally, or unintentionally?
MELETUS. Intentionally, I say.

div.head: Section 26
div.p: SOCRATES. What is this, Meletus? Are you so much wiser at your age than I am at mine, that you have recognized that the bad always do some evil to those closest to them, and the good do good; whereas I have reached such a depth of ignorance that I do not even know that if I make one of my associates wicked, I risk being harmed by him, and yet I commit this great evil intentionally, as you claim? I do not believe you, Meletus, and I think no other human being does either. Rather, either I do not corrupt them, or if I do corrupt them, I do so unintentionally. So in either case, you are lying. And if I corrupt them unintentionally, the law does not require bringing people to court for such unintentional errors, but taking them aside privately to teach and admonish them. For it is clear that if I learn better, I will stop doing what I do unintentionally. But you avoided associating with me and teaching me; you did not want to do it. Instead, you brought me here to court, where the law says those should be brought who need punishment, not instruction. It is already clear, men of Athens, what I was saying: Meletus has never cared about these things, neither greatly nor slightly. Nevertheless, tell us, Meletus, in what way do you say I corrupt the youth? Or is it clear from the indictment you wrote that it is by teaching them not to believe in the gods the city believes in, but in other new spiritual things? Do you not say that I corrupt them by teaching these things?
MELETUS. I most certainly say that.

SOCRATES. Then by those very gods we are discussing, Meletus, clarify this further for me and for these men. I cannot understand whether you are saying I teach them to believe in certain gods—in which case I do believe there are gods and am not entirely an atheist, nor am I guilty of that, but simply that they are not the gods the city believes in, but different ones, and this is your charge against me, that they are different—or whether you are saying that I do not believe in gods at all myself, and that I teach this atheism to others.
MELETUS. That is what I say: you do not believe in gods at all.
SOCRATES. Marvelous Meletus, why do you say this? Do I not even believe that the sun and moon are gods, as the rest of mankind does?
MELETUS. By Zeus, judges, he does not! He says the sun is stone and the moon is earth.

SOCRATES. Do you think you are prosecuting Anaxagoras, my dear Meletus? Do you despise these men so much, and consider them so illiterate, that you think they do not know the books of Anaxagoras of Clazomenae are full of these theories? And the young men learn these things from me, when they can buy the books in the orchestra for a drachma at most, and laugh at Socrates if he claims these ideas as his own, especially since they are so strange? But tell me, by Zeus, do you really think I believe there is no god?
MELETUS. You do not, by Zeus, not at all.

div.head: Section 27
div.p: SOCRATES. You are unbelievable, Meletus, and I think you do not even believe yourself. It seems to me, men of Athens, that this man is highly insolent and unrestrained, and that he wrote this indictment simply out of youthfulness and rashness. He seems to be testing me by posing a riddle: "Will the wise Socrates realize that I am joking and contradicting myself, or will I deceive him and the rest of the listeners?" For he appears to contradict himself in the indictment, as if he were saying: "Socrates acts unjustly by not believing in gods, but by believing in gods." But this is the conduct of a joker. Consider with me, gentlemen, how he appears to say this. And you, Meletus, answer us. You others, please remember my request not to make a disturbance if I conduct the argument in my usual manner. Is there any human being, Meletus, who believes that human matters exist, but does not believe in humans?
MELETUS. ...

SOCRATES. Let him answer, gentlemen, and not cause disturbance after disturbance! Is there anyone who does not believe in horses, but believes in equine matters? Or does not believe there are flute-players, but believes in flute-playing matters? There is no one, best of men. If you are not willing to answer, I will tell you and these men. But answer at least the next question: is there anyone who believes spiritual matters exist, but does not believe in spirits?
MELETUS. There is not.

SOCRATES. How helpful that you finally answered under compulsion by these men! Now, you say in your indictment that I believe in and teach spiritual things, whether new or old; at any rate, I believe in spiritual things according to your own statement, which you swore to in the indictment. But if I believe in spiritual things, there is a strong necessity that I must also believe in spirits. Is this not so? It is. I assume you agree, since you do not answer. And do we not believe that spirits are either gods or the children of gods? Do you say yes or no?
MELETUS. Yes.

SOCRATES. Then if I believe in spirits, as you say, and if spirits are a kind of god, this is what I mean when I say you are joking and posing a riddle: you state that I do not believe in gods, but then again that I do believe in gods, since I believe in spirits. On the other hand, if spirits are the bastard children of gods—whether by nymphs or some other mothers as they say—what human being could believe that the children of gods exist, but that gods do not? It would be as absurd as believing in the children of horses and asses—mules—but not believing that horses and asses exist. No, Meletus, there is no way you wrote this indictment except to test us, or because you were at a loss as to what true injustice you could charge me with. You could never persuade any human being with even a little intelligence that the same person could believe in spiritual and divine things, and then again that this same person could believe there are no spirits, no gods, and no heroes.

div.head: Section 28
div.p: In truth, men of Athens, I do not think it requires a long defense to prove that I am not unjust according to Meletus's indictment. What has been said is sufficient. But as I said earlier, I have incurred much hatred among many people, and you know well that this is true. And this is what will convict me, if it does convict me: not Meletus, nor Anytus, but the prejudice and envy of the multitude, which has convicted many other good men, and will likely continue to do so. There is no danger that it will stop with me. Perhaps someone might say: "Are you not ashamed, Socrates, to have pursued an occupation that has now put you at risk of death?" I would answer him with a just reply: "You speak poorly, my friend, if you think a man of any worth at all ought to calculate the risk of living or dying, and not consider only this: whether the things he does are just or unjust, the deeds of a good man or a bad one. According to your reasoning, the demigods who died at Troy would be worthless, especially the son of Thetis (Achilles). He despised danger so much compared to enduring shame that when his mother, a goddess, saw him eager to kill Hector, she spoke to him—I think it went something like this: 'My son, if you avenge the murder of your comrade Patroclus and kill Hector, you yourself will die, for your doom is ready straightaway after Hector.' Hearing this, he belittled death and danger. Fearing far more to live as a coward and not avenge his friends, he said, 'May I die straightaway, after inflicting justice on the wrongdoer, so that I may not remain here by the curved ships, an object of ridicule, a burden on the earth.' Do you think he gave a thought to death or danger?" This is the truth, men of Athens: wherever a man places himself, believing it is the best, or wherever he is placed by a commander, there he must stay and face danger, taking no account of death or anything else before shame. For me to do otherwise would be terrible indeed. When the commanders you elected to command me stationed me at Potidaea, Amphipolis, and Delium, I remained where they posted me and faced the risk of death like anyone else. So if the god stationed me—as I believed and understood—with the command that I must live a life of philosophy, examining myself and others, it would be a terrible thing if I were to abandon my post because of the fear of death or anything else.

div.head: Section 29
div.p: It would be terrible, and truly someone might then justly bring me to court for not believing there are gods, since I disobeyed the oracle, feared death, and thought myself wise when I was not. For to fear death, gentlemen, is nothing other than to think oneself wise when one is not, for it is to think one knows what one does not know. No one knows whether death might not be the greatest of all blessings for a human being, yet they fear it as if they knew well that it is the greatest of evils. Is this not that most shameful ignorance: thinking one knows what one does not know? Here too, gentlemen, I differ perhaps from most men. If I were to say I am wiser than anyone in anything, it would be in this: that since I do not have adequate knowledge about the things in Hades, I do not think I know. But I do know that it is evil and shameful to do wrong and to disobey one's superior, whether god or man. Therefore, I will never fear or flee from things that might be good, rather than avoiding what I know to be evil. So even if you acquit me now and do not listen to Anytus—who said I should either never have been brought to court, or, having been brought, must be put to death, warning you that if I escape, your sons will practice what Socrates teaches and be utterly corrupted—if you were to say to me, "Socrates, we will not listen to Anytus, and we acquit you, but on this condition: that you no longer spend your time in this investigation or practice philosophy, and if you are caught doing so again, you will die"—if you were to acquit me on these terms, I would say to you: "Men of Athens, I welcome and love you, but I will obey the god rather than you. As long as I draw breath and am able, I will not stop practicing philosophy, exhorting you, and showing the truth to anyone I happen to meet. I will say what I always say: 'Best of men, you are an Athenian, from the greatest city with the greatest reputation for wisdom and power. Are you not ashamed to care about acquiring as much money, reputation, and honor as possible, while you do not care or think about wisdom, truth, and making your soul as good as possible?' And if any of you disputes this and says he does care, I will not let him go immediately or leave him, but I will question him, examine him, and cross-examine him. And if he seems not to possess virtue, but only claims to, I will reproach him for valuing the most important things the least, and the trivial things the most. I will do this to young and old, foreigner and citizen, but especially to the citizens, since you are closer to me in kin."

div.head: Section 30
div.p: Know well that this is what the god commands. And I believe there has never been a greater blessing for the city than my service to the god. For I do nothing but go about persuading you, both young and old, not to care for your bodies or your money as intensely as you care for making your soul as good as possible. I tell you that virtue does not come from money, but that from virtue comes money and all other good things for men, both privately and publicly. If by saying these things I corrupt the youth, then these teachings must be harmful. But if anyone says I say anything other than this, he is talking nonsense. Therefore I say to you, men of Athens: obey Anytus or not, acquit me or not, knowing that I will not change my conduct, not even if I am to die many times over. Do not make a disturbance, men of Athens, but abide by my request not to cry out at what I say, but to listen. I think you will benefit from listening. I am going to say something else to you at which you might cry out; but please do not do so. Know well that if you put me to death, being the kind of man I say I am, you will not harm me more than you harm yourselves. Meletus or Anytus could not harm me; it is impossible, for I do not think it is permitted for a better man to be harmed by a worse one. He might kill me, or banish me, or disenfranchise me, and he and others may think these are great evils. But I do not think so. It is a much greater evil to do what he is doing now: attempting to kill a man unjustly. Therefore, men of Athens, I am far from making a defense for my own sake, as one might think. I am defending you, so that you do not err concerning the god's gift to you by condemning me. For if you kill me, you will not easily find another like me. I have been literally attached to the city by the god—if it is not too ridiculous to say—as upon a great and noble horse which is rather sluggish because of its size and needs to be awakened by a gadfly. I believe the god has attached me to the city as just such a gadfly, awakening, persuading, and reproaching each one of you, never stopping all day long, settling everywhere upon you. Another like me will not easily come to you, gentlemen, and if you listen to me, you will spare me. But perhaps you may become annoyed, like people awakened from sleep, and slapping me as Anytus advises, you might easily kill me. Then you would sleep for the rest of your lives, unless the god, caring for you, sends you someone else.

div.head: Section 31
div.p: To recognize that I am such a man given to the city by the god, consider this: it does not seem human that I should have neglected all my own affairs and endured seeing my household neglected all these years, while always doing your business, approaching each of you privately like a father or an older brother, persuading you to care for virtue. If I derived any profit from this and received pay for my exhortations, there would be some reason in it. But as it is, you yourselves see that my accusers, who have so shamelessly accused me of everything else, could not summon the shamelessness to provide a witness claiming I ever demanded or received pay. I offer a sufficient witness, I think, that I am speaking the truth: my poverty. Perhaps it may seem strange that I give this advice going around privately and meddling in other people's affairs, but do not dare to go before your assembly publicly and advise the city. The reason for this is what you have heard me say many times and in many places: that a certain divine and spiritual voice comes to me, the very thing Meletus mocked in his indictment. It has been coming to me since childhood; it is a voice that, whenever it comes, always turns me away from what I am about to do, but never turns me forward. This is what opposes my involvement in politics. And I think it opposes me very well. For know well, men of Athens, that if I had attempted to engage in politics long ago, I would have died long ago and been of no use to you or to myself. Do not be angry with me for speaking the truth: no man will survive if he genuinely opposes you or any other multitude and prevents many unjust and illegal things from happening in the city. A man who truly fights for justice, if he is to survive even for a short time, must remain a private citizen and not a public one.

div.head: Section 32
div.p: I will give you powerful proofs of these things—not words, but what you value: deeds. Listen to what happened to me, so you may see that I would never yield to anyone against justice through fear of death, even if I were to perish by not yielding. I will tell you things commonly heard in the law courts, perhaps tiresome, but true. I have never held any public office in the city, men of Athens, except being a member of the Council. Our tribe, Antiochis, happened to hold the prytany when you decided to judge the ten generals who had not picked up the survivors of the naval battle. You judged them all together, which was illegal, as you all recognized later. But at the time, I was the only prytanis who opposed you doing anything contrary to the laws, and I voted against it. Even though the orators were ready to indict and arrest me, and you were shouting and urging them on, I thought I had to run the risk with law and justice rather than side with you in an unjust decision because of fear of prison or death. This happened while the city was still a democracy. When the oligarchy was established, the Thirty summoned me and four others to the Rotunda, and ordered us to bring Leon the Salaminian from Salamis to be put to death. They gave many such orders to many people, wishing to implicate as many as possible in their guilt. But there again, I demonstrated—not in word, but in deed—that I do not care about death in the slightest (if that is not too rustic a way of putting it). But I care entirely about doing nothing unjust or impious. That government, strong as it was, did not terrify me into doing an unjust act. When we came out of the Rotunda, the other four went to Salamis and brought Leon, but I departed and went home. I might have been put to death for that, if that government had not fallen soon after. There are many who will testify to you about these things.

div.head: Section 33
div.p: Do you think I would have survived so many years if I had engaged in public affairs and, acting as a good man must, supported just causes and made that my highest priority? Far from it, men of Athens; nor would any other man. But throughout my entire life, whether acting publicly—if I ever did—or privately, you will find I am always the same man, never yielding to anyone contrary to justice, not even to one of those my slanderers claim are my pupils. I have never been anyone's teacher. If anyone, young or old, desired to listen to me while I was speaking and doing my own work, I never begrudged it to anyone. I do not converse only when I receive money and refuse when I do not. Rather, I offer myself equally to the rich and the poor to question, and to listen and answer if anyone wishes. If any of these people becomes a good man or not, I cannot justly be held responsible, since I never promised to teach any of them anything, nor did I teach them. If anyone says he ever learned or heard anything privately from me that everyone else did not hear, know well that he is not speaking the truth. Why, then, do some people enjoy spending so much time with me? You have heard the reason, men of Athens. I told you the whole truth: they enjoy hearing the cross-examination of those who think they are wise but are not. For it is not unpleasant. And as I say, I have been commanded by the god to do this, through oracles, dreams, and every way any divine apportionment has ever commanded a human being to do anything. This is true, men of Athens, and easily proven. If I am currently corrupting some of the youth, and have already corrupted others, surely some of those who are now older and have realized that I gave them bad advice when they were young should come forward now to accuse me and exact punishment. Or if they did not wish to, some of their relatives—fathers, brothers, or other kin—should remember and exact punishment now, if their relatives suffered any harm from me.

div.head: Section 34
div.p: In any case, many of them are present here, whom I can see. First, Crito is here, of my own age and deme, the father of Critobulus here. Then Lysanias the Sphettian, the father of Aeschines here. Also Antiphon of Cephisia, the father of Epigenes. Then there are those whose brothers associated with me: Nicostratus the son of Theozotides, brother of Theodotus (and Theodotus is dead, so he could not have begged his brother to stop); and Paralius the son of Demodocus, whose brother was Theages. And Adeimantus the son of Ariston, whose brother is Plato here; and Aiantodorus, whose brother is Apollodorus here. I could name many others. Meletus ought to have produced at least one of them as a witness during his speech. If he forgot then, let him produce one now—I yield the floor—and let him say if he has any such witness. But you will find it is entirely the opposite, gentlemen. They are all ready to help me, the corrupter, the one who harmed their relatives, as Meletus and Anytus claim. Perhaps the corrupted themselves might have some reason to help me. But the uncorrupted, the older relatives—what reason could they have to help me, other than the right and just reason: that they know Meletus is lying, and I am speaking the truth? Well then, gentlemen. These, and perhaps other similar things, are what I could say in my defense. Perhaps one of you may be angry when he remembers his own case, if he was on trial for a lesser charge than this and begged and entreated the judges with many tears, bringing his children, relatives, and many friends up here to arouse as much pity as possible. Yet I will do none of these things, even though I am running the ultimate risk, as it may seem. Thinking of this, he might become stubborn toward me and, angered by this very fact, cast his vote in anger. If any of you feels this way—I do not expect you do, but if you do—it seems reasonable for me to say: "My friend, I too have a family. I am not born of oak or rock, as Homer says, but of human beings." So I do have a family, and three sons, men of Athens: one is a youth, and two are still boys. Nevertheless, I will not bring any of them here to beg you to acquit me.

div.head: Section 35
div.p: Why will I not do any of these things? Not out of stubbornness, men of Athens, nor out of disrespect for you. Whether I am bold in the face of death or not is another matter. But for the sake of reputation—mine, yours, and the whole city's—it does not seem right for me to do such things at my age and with my reputation, whether true or false; for it is generally believed that Socrates is somehow superior to the majority of men. If those of you who seem superior in wisdom, courage, or any other virtue were to act this way, it would be shameful. I have seen men who were thought to be somebody do strange things when on trial, as if they thought suffering death would be a terrible thing, and as if they would be immortal if you did not kill them. They seem to bring shame upon the city, so that a stranger might assume that the men of Athens who excel in virtue, whom the Athenians themselves select for offices and honors, are no different from women. Those of you who are thought to be anybody at all should not do these things; and if we try to do them, you should not permit it. You should make it clear that you are much more likely to convict the man who stages these pitiful scenes and makes the city an object of ridicule than the man who remains quiet. Apart from reputation, gentlemen, it does not seem just to me to beg the judge or to be acquitted by begging, but rather to teach and persuade. The judge does not sit here to grant justice as a favor, but to judge what is just. He has sworn an oath not to grant favors to whoever he pleases, but to judge according to the laws. Therefore, we should not habituate you to breaking your oath, nor should you become habituated to it, for then neither of us would be acting piously. Do not ask me, men of Athens, to do before you things I consider neither honorable, nor just, nor pious—especially, by Zeus, when I am being prosecuted for impiety by Meletus here! For clearly, if I persuaded you and forced you by begging against your oaths, I would be teaching you not to believe there are gods, and by making my defense I would be simply accusing myself of not believing in the gods. But that is far from the truth. I do believe in them, men of Athens, in a way none of my accusers do. And I entrust it to you and to the god to judge me in the way that will be best for me and for you.

div.head: Section 36
div.p: If I am not upset by the outcome of your vote, men of Athens—by your condemning me—there are many reasons for this, but particularly because this event did not come as a surprise. I am much more surprised by the number of votes cast on each side. I did not think the margin would be so narrow; I expected it to be much wider. But as it is, it seems that if only thirty votes had crossed over, I would have been acquitted. In fact, as far as Meletus is concerned, I consider that I have been acquitted even now. And not only acquitted, but it is clear to everyone that if Anytus and Lycon had not come forward to accuse me, he would have been fined a thousand drachmas for not getting a fifth of the votes. The man proposes the penalty of death for me. Very well. What counter-penalty shall I propose to you, men of Athens? Clearly, what I deserve. What then? What do I deserve to suffer or pay, because I did not keep quiet during my life, but neglected what most people care about—moneymaking, household management, generalships, public speaking, and the other offices and factions in the city—thinking myself truly too honest to survive if I engaged in those things? I did not go where I would be of no use to you or myself. Instead, I went to each of you privately to confer what I say is the greatest benefit, trying to persuade each of you not to care for any of his belongings before caring for himself, to be as good and wise as possible, nor to care for the city's belongings before the city itself, and to care for other things in the same way. What do I deserve, being such a man? Something good, men of Athens, if I must propose what I truly deserve according to my worth. And a good that would be suitable for me. What is suitable for a poor benefactor who needs leisure to exhort you? Nothing is more suitable, men of Athens, than for such a man to be given free meals in the Prytaneum. He deserves this much more than any of you who has won a victory at Olympia with a horse or chariot. The victor makes you think you are happy, but I make you truly happy. And he does not need the food, but I do. So if I must propose a penalty according to my just deserts, I propose this: free meals in the Prytaneum.

div.head: Section 37
div.p: Perhaps when I say this, you will think I am speaking out of stubbornness, just as when I spoke about wailing and begging. But it is not that, men of Athens. Rather, I am convinced that I do not intentionally wrong any human being. However, I have not persuaded you of this, because we have conversed for so little time. If it were the law here, as in other cities, to judge a trial for life not in a single day but over several days, I think you would have been persuaded. But as it is, it is not easy to dispel great slanders in a short time. Being convinced that I do no wrong to anyone, I am certainly not going to wrong myself and say against myself that I deserve something bad, and propose such a penalty for myself. Out of fear of what? Fearing I might suffer the penalty Meletus proposes, when I say I do not know whether it is good or bad? Should I choose instead something I know perfectly well is bad, and propose that? Prison? Why should I live in prison, a slave to the presiding magistrates, the Eleven? A fine? And imprisonment until I pay? That would be the same as I just said, because I have no money to pay. Should I propose exile? Perhaps you would accept that penalty. I would have to be deeply in love with life, men of Athens, to be so irrational as not to realize that if you, my fellow citizens, could not endure my company and my words, but found them too burdensome and hateful, and seek to be rid of them now—will others endure them easily? Far from it, men of Athens. It would be a fine life for a man of my age to leave his city and live wandering from city to city, constantly being driven out. For I know well that wherever I go, the young men will listen to my talk, just as they do here. If I drive them away, they will persuade their elders to expel me. If I do not drive them away, their fathers and relatives will expel me for their sakes.

div.head: Section 38
div.p: Perhaps someone might say: "Socrates, can you not just leave us and live a quiet life, keeping silent?" This is the hardest thing of all to persuade some of you to believe. If I say that this is disobeying the god, and that therefore I cannot keep quiet, you will not believe me and will think I am being ironic. If I say that the greatest good for a human being is to discuss virtue every day, and the other things you hear me conversing and examining myself and others about, and that the unexamined life is not worth living for a human being—you will believe me even less. Yet these things are as I say, gentlemen, though it is not easy to persuade you. Furthermore, I am not accustomed to thinking I deserve anything bad. If I had money, I would propose a fine as large as I could pay, for that would not harm me. But as it is, I have none, unless you are willing to set a fine at an amount I could actually pay. Perhaps I could pay you a mina of silver. So I propose that amount. Wait, Plato here, men of Athens, along with Crito, Critobulus, and Apollodorus, bid me propose a penalty of thirty minae, and they offer themselves as guarantors. So I propose that amount, and they will be reliable guarantors of the money for you.

div.head: Section 39
div.p: For the sake of a short amount of time, men of Athens, you will gain the reputation and the blame, from those who want to revile the city, of having killed Socrates, a wise man. For those who want to reproach you will say I am wise, even if I am not. If you had waited just a little while, this would have happened on its own. For you see my age, that it is far advanced in life and close to death. I say this not to all of you, but to those who voted to condemn me to death. And I have something else to say to these same men. Perhaps you think, men of Athens, that I was convicted because of a lack of words to persuade you, if I had thought it right to do and say everything to escape the penalty. Far from it. I was convicted for a lack, but not of words. Rather, a lack of boldness and shamelessness, and an unwillingness to say the things you find most pleasant to hear: wailing and lamenting, and doing and saying many other things unworthy of me, which you are accustomed to hearing from others. But I did not think then that I should do anything unworthy of a free man because of the danger, nor do I now regret making my defense the way I did. I much prefer to die after defending myself in that way, than to live by defending myself in yours. Neither in a law court nor in war should I or anyone else contrive a way to escape death at any cost. In battles, it is often clear that a man might escape death by throwing down his weapons and turning to supplicate his pursuers. And there are many other ways to escape death in dangers, if a man dares to do and say anything. The difficult thing, gentlemen, is not escaping death; escaping wickedness is much more difficult, for it runs faster than death. And now I, being slow and old, have been caught by the slower runner; while my accusers, being clever and quick, have been caught by the faster runner: wickedness. And now I depart, condemned by you to suffer the penalty of death, while they depart, condemned by truth to suffer wickedness and injustice. I abide by my penalty, and they by theirs. Perhaps these things had to happen this way, and I think it is for the best.

div.head: Section 40
div.p: Next, I desire to prophesy to you who condemned me. For I am now at the point where men most prophesy—when they are about to die. I say to you, the men who have condemned me, that punishment will come upon you immediately after my death, a punishment far harsher, by Zeus, than the death you have imposed on me. You have done this thinking you will be freed from having to give an account of your lives. But the result will be entirely the opposite, I promise you. There will be more people to demand an account from you, men whom I was holding back, though you did not notice it. And they will be harsher, because they are younger, and you will be even more annoyed. If you think that by putting men to death you can stop people from reproaching you for not living correctly, you are not thinking straight. That kind of escape is neither entirely possible nor honorable. The best and easiest way is not to suppress others, but to prepare oneself to be as good as possible. With this prophecy to those who voted against me, I depart. But as for those who voted for my acquittal, I would gladly converse with you about this thing that has just happened, while the magistrates are busy and I have not yet gone to the place where I must die. Please stay with me, gentlemen, for this short time. Nothing prevents us from talking to one another while we can. I want to show you, as my friends, what the meaning of this current event is. Something wondrous has happened to me, judges—for by calling you judges I speak correctly. The prophetic voice of my divine sign was constantly opposing me in previous times, even in very small matters, if I was about to do something incorrectly. But now, as you can see, something has happened to me that might be thought the greatest of evils. Yet the sign of the god did not oppose me when I left my house this morning, nor when I stepped up here to the court, nor anywhere in my speech when I was about to say something. In other speeches, it has stopped me in mid-sentence. But today, regarding this affair, it has opposed me in no deed or word. What do I suppose is the cause? I will tell you. It is likely that what has happened to me is a good thing, and those of us who suppose that death is an evil are not thinking correctly. I have great proof of this: my customary sign would surely have opposed me if I were not about to accomplish something good.

div.head: Section 41
div.p: Let us also consider how great a hope there is that death is a good thing. For death is one of two things: either it is a state of nothingness and utter unconsciousness for the dead man, or, according to what people say, it is a change and a migration of the soul from this place to another. If it is unconsciousness, like a sleep in which the sleeper sees no dreams, death would be a wondrous gain. I think if a man were to select the night he slept so soundly he did not even dream, and compare it with the other nights and days of his life, and had to declare how many days and nights he had lived better and more pleasantly than that one night, I think that not only a private citizen, but the Great King himself would find them easy to count compared to the others. If death is like that, I call it a gain, for all eternity would seem no longer than a single night. If, on the other hand, death is a journey from here to another place, and the stories are true that all the dead are there, what greater good could there be than this, judges? If upon arriving in Hades, having escaped these self-styled judges here, one finds the true judges who are said to sit in judgment there—Minos, Rhadamanthys, Aeacus, and Triptolemus, and other demigods who were just in their own lives—would that be a bad journey? Or to associate with Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod, and Homer—how much would any of you pay for that? I am willing to die many times over if these things are true. For my own part, the conversations there would be wondrous, meeting Palamedes and Ajax the son of Telamon, and anyone else from ancient times who died through an unjust judgment. Comparing my experiences with theirs would not be unpleasant, I think. And the greatest pleasure would be spending my time examining and questioning the people there, just as I do here, finding out who among them is wise, and who thinks he is but is not. How much would one pay, judges, to examine the man who led the great army against Troy, or Odysseus, or Sisyphus, and countless other men and women? To converse with them, associate with them, and examine them there would be an unimaginable happiness. Surely those there do not put people to death for it! They are happier than the people here in every way, and for the rest of time they are immortal, if the stories are true.

div.head: Section 42
div.p: You too must have good hope towards death, judges, and hold this one truth in mind: that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death, and his affairs are not neglected by the gods. My current situation has not happened by chance; it is clear to me that it was better for me to die now and be released from my troubles. That is why the divine sign did not turn me back, and why I am not entirely angry with those who condemned me or with my accusers. Though they did not condemn and accuse me with this intention, but thinking they would harm me, for which they deserve blame. However, I beg this one thing from them: when my sons grow up, punish them, gentlemen, and pain them in the very same way I pained you, if they seem to you to care about money or anything else before virtue. And if they think they are somebody when they are nobody, reproach them just as I reproached you, that they do not care for what they should, and think they are something when they are worth nothing. If you do this, I will have received justice from you, both I and my sons. But now it is time to depart. For me to die, and for you to live. Which of us goes to the better thing is unclear to everyone, except the god.
